source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Stop metoprolol abruptly once blood pressure is controlled, because chronic beta-blocker therapy does not require tapering when angina is stable.","B":"Avoid abrupt discontinuation; chronic metoprolol should generally be reduced over 1–2 weeks because sudden withdrawal can worsen angina or precipitate ischemia.","C":"Replace metoprolol immediately with a stimulant medication, because abrupt beta-blocker withdrawal primarily causes persistent symptomatic bradycardia and fatigue.","D":"Skip alternate doses for one day and then stop completely, because a 24-hour reduction is sufficient to prevent withdrawal-related myocardial ischemia."}}
source_row.rationale: Current metoprolol labeling warns that abrupt cessation of chronic therapy can exacerbate angina and has been associated with myocardial infarction; it recommends gradual dose reduction over 1–2 weeks with monitoring. Option B reflects that warning. Option A encourages abrupt cessation. Option C gives an inappropriate substitute and misstates the withdrawal concern. Option D provides an inadequate taper.
